items.title: AI is Reshaping the Role of Academic Librarians; Elsevier Releases Librarian of the Future Report
items.raw_text: From an Elsevier News Release: Today, Elsevier shares findings from its global Librarian of the Future research, revealing how artificial intelligence (AI) and changing research needs are reshaping the role of academic librarians. Drawing on insights from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders, the report reveals a profession harnessing AI while also anticipating a greater role in helping institutions navigate its risks. The findings point to an opportunity for librarians to become more closely involved in institutional decision-making and strengthen their position as strategic partners in research. [Clip] Librarians expect their role in AI to grow meaningfully. Almost all (95%) expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years, while 82% believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers and 76% believe they should play a role in AI governance. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) While librarians are ready to contribute to AI initiatives, only 30% report their institution has implemented an AI policy. These findings highlight a potential gap between the pace of AI adoption and institutional preparedness. With this in mind, the report points to an increasingly important role for librarians in helping researchers navigate trusted information, responsible AI use and research integrity. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) Jim O’Donnell, University Librarian

items.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
items.raw_text: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. items.raw_text: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. items.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
items.raw_text: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates . Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.raw_text: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

items.raw_text: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search . Read full article Comments

items.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
items.raw_text: The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. Read full article Comments

items.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
items.raw_text: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Read full article Comments

items.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
items.raw_text: Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania , one in New York , and one in Wisconsin . Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania's health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state's seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County , but state health officials have not confirmed it. For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they're the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania's case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650. Read full article Comments

items.title: Als verdwijnt wat ons beschermd
items.raw_text: In Europa staan belangrijke rechten nog steeds onder druk dankzij de verschillende omnibussen. Dat zijn wetsvoorstellen waarmee, via een versneld proces, Europese wetten ‘versimpeld’ moeten worden. Denk daarbij aan wetten die over onze gezondheid, veiligheid en leefomgeving gaan, maar ook over onze privacy. Onze rechten op de onderhandelingstafel Door middel van digitale omnibussen worden belangrijke wetten, waaronder de AI-verordening en de Algemene verordening gegevensbescherming afgezwakt onder het mom van ‘versimpeling van administratieve lasten’. Eerder dit jaar werd er al een knoop doorgehakt over de wijzigingen in de AI-verordening. Net voordat de wet in werking zou treden, werd de wet al gewijzigd en werd de implementatietermijn uitgesteld. Hierdoor treedt de wet die AI in Europa moet reguleren nóg later in werking, terwijl de ontwikkeling daarvan in razend tempo doorgaat. Over wijzigingen die onder andere over de Algemene verordening gegevensbescherming gaan, wordt nog volop onderhandeld. Op 21 oktober heeft de Raad van de Europese Unie namens de Europese lidstaten een positie ingenomen. Nu is het aan het Europees Parlement om een positie in te nemen. Vervolgens zullen de triloog onderhandelingen plaatsvinden tussen de Europese Commissie, de Raad van de Europese Unie en het Europees Parlement. items.title: Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools
items.raw_text: Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral. Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse. You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control. Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time. We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org. For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools ). Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities.

items.title: UvA-onderzoekers kritisch op EU-voorstel digitale autonomie
items.raw_text: Het Europese voorstel voor een Cloud and AI Development Act (Cada) is niet ambitieus genoeg om de digitale autonomie van Europa te vergroten. De onderzoekers van het Instituut voor Informatierecht (IViR) van de Universiteit van Amsterdam stellen dat na een analyse van de Cada. Dit voorstel voor een Cada beoogt de Europese cloud- en ai-sector te versterken en de afhankelijkheid van Amerikaanse aanbieders te verkleinen. Volgens de onderzoekers schiet het echter tekort. Bovendien roepen de snelle uitbreiding van datacenters en de beperkte aandacht voor duurzaamheid en maatschappelijke impact bij hun zorgen op. De EU zoekt het in meer aantrekkelijke investeringsvoorwaarden voor grootschalige uitbreiding van datacenters. Tegelijkertijd moeten er regels komen voor de inkoop van clouddiensten door de overheid. Maar de onderzoekers vinden dat de EU daar niet ver genoeg in gaat. Belemmerd Zij tellen dat overheden bij veel diensten beperkt worden in de mogelijkheid om extra eisen te stellen en zo hun afhankelijkheid te verminderen. ‘Zoals het er nu voorstaat, zou dit EU-voorstel overheidsinstellingen zelfs tegenhouden als ze bewust voor een Europees alternatief willen kiezen’, aldus onderzoekster Kristina Irion. Zij vreest dat het streven naar digitale autonomie zelfs door Cada kan worden belemmerd. Deze act koppelt strengere eisen aan clouddiensten aan het risiconiveau van overheidstaken. items.title: Snowflake brengt bedrijfs- en pro­duct­be­vei­li­ging onder één dak
items.raw_text: Snowflake heeft de beveiliging van het eigen bedrijf en die van zijn platform onder één verantwoordelijke gebracht. Die rol ligt sinds januari bij Mayank Upadhyay, chief security and trust officer. Hij sprak met Computable tijdens zijn bezoek aan Rotterdam. Upadhyay werkte 21 jaar bij Google, laatst als vp van het beveiligingsplatform van Google Cloud . Naar eigen zeggen leidde zijn team er onder meer werk aan zero trust, tweestapsverificatie, Fido en passkeys. Zijn overstap verklaart hij vanuit de data: modellen komen van overal, maar de data maakt het verschil. Het mandaat omvat volgens Upadhyay een ‘dubbele scope’: Snowflake zelf beveiligen en klanten helpen het platform veilig in te richten en te gebruiken. Die combinatie ontstond na zijn komst. Hij noemt het logisch bij een platformaanbieder. Een probleem op het platform raakt meerdere klanten tegelijk, waardoor beveiliging volgens hem lastig bij een externe leverancier onder te brengen is. Bovendien zou het leveranciersaanbod de specifieke eisen niet altijd bijhouden. Snowflake draait naar eigen zeggen volledig op zijn eigen platform (‘Snow on Snow’). Dat vraagt wat van it. ‘It-managers moeten daarom nu al nadenken over aeo, nog voordat marketing daarom vraagt’, stelt Jessica Jacobs van Incubeta.
